resources.string: Overview and planning
The project is a whole compiler, but it's five little programs that talk to each other. Plan before you code.

Week 3 of the semester. The assignment lands on Canvas: 'Build a complete compiler for a simple imperative language, in Java, generating MIPS assembly that runs on MARS'. You read it twice. Then you read it again.
A WHOLE compiler? I can barely write a for loop in Java without looking it up…
Breathe. Nobody writes a compiler in one go. You'll write **five small pieces** that talk to each other, and you've already practiced each one here in Compilândia.
Each station on the conveyor becomes a Java class in your project.
The project's pieces (and the Java file for each)
**Lexical** (`Lexico.java`): text → tokens. A DFA written with a `switch` over states.
**Syntactic** (`Sintatico.java`): tokens → 'is the program well-formed?'. Recursive descent: one method per nonterminal.
**Semantic** (`TabelaSimbolos.java` + checks inside `Sintatico`): was it declared? does the type fit?
**Generator** (also inside `Sintatico`): each method emits its own piece of MIPS assembly.
**Optimization** (optional/bonus): fold constants, cut dead code.
**Tests**: one folder of programs that MUST compile and another of programs that MUST fail.

Notice a detail: semantic and generator live **inside** the syntactic phase. It's **one-pass syntax-directed translation**: the parser asks the scanner for a token when it needs one, checks the semantics on the spot and spits out MIPS right away. No giant tree in memory, no second pass. It's the shape that fits a one-semester project.
Suggested folder structure
ErroCompilacao.java: EVERY compiler error goes through here, always with the line
Main.java: the conductor (Java 17)
Which implementation order causes the LEAST headache?
Write everything at once and test in the last week
Lexical → syntactic → semantic → generation, testing each phase before moving on
Start with MIPS generation, which is worth the most points
Start with the symbol table, which everyone uses
Each phase CONSUMES the previous one's output. If the scanner has a bug, the parser looks broken without being broken. Build from the bottom up and test each layer before stacking the next one.
8-week schedule (adjust it to your assignment's date)
Week 1: Define the language and write 10 sample programs (5 right, 5 with errors).
Week 2: Scanner + a `TesteLexico` that prints the tokens.
Weeks 3–4: LL(1) grammar on paper (FIRST/FOLLOW!) and the top-down parser.
Week 5: Symbol table and type checking.
Weeks 6–7: MIPS generation, testing each statement on MARS.
Week 8: Optimization, test suite, report. And some slack: something ALWAYS runs late.
Git from day 1: one branch per phase, small commits
Small commits save lives: when code generation breaks the parser at 11 p.m., `git diff` shows exactly what changed. And the commit history proves the work belongs to the team.
A pair? One starts the scanner while the other writes the grammar on paper. A trio? The third writes the test suite from day one.
But watch out: **everyone** needs to understand **everything**. At the oral exam, the professor points at any method and asks any member 'why is this here?'.

Read the assignment with a highlighter. Error message format, output file name, whether it stops at the first error, whether keywords ignore case… Some professors grade with scripts that compare the output character by character; one extra space becomes 'test failed'.

Q: Can I use ANTLR, JavaCC or another generator? A: In most classes, NO, the goal is to write the scanner and parser by hand. In some places the scanner is done with lex/flex (the app's Flex Workshop trains that). When in doubt, ask the professor BEFORE you start.
In one sentence: what does your `Main` do?

It reads the source file, hands it to `Sintatico` (which pulls tokens from `Lexico`, checks `TabelaSimbolos` and emits MIPS) and writes the `.asm`: or prints the line and the message of the first error.
Slow… and steady… one phase… at a time.
Defining the Byteiro language
Before Java: tokens, precedence and an informal grammar for a small, complete language.

Before a single line of Java, you need a language. In the project the class invents (or receives) its own. In this guide we'll invent **Byteiro**: tiny on purpose. Its keywords are in Portuguese, as in the original course.
Can I add classes, lambdas, arrays, recursive functions…?
NO. Each extra feature is one more chapter of pain. **Small and complete beats big and broken.** Functions and arrays go under 'future work' in the report.
contagem.byt: a complete Byteiro program (we'll compile it all the way to MIPS in chapter 8)
Byteiro fact sheet
**Types**: `inteiro` (integer, 32 bits), `logico` (boolean: `verdadeiro`/`falso`), `caractere` (character: `'A'`).
**Statements**: declaration (`inteiro a, b;`), assignment with `<-`, `se`/`senao` (if/else), `enquanto` (while), `escreva(...)` (write), `leia(x)` (read).
**Expressions**: arithmetic `+ - * / %`, relational `= <> < > <= >=`, logical `e ou nao` (and, or, not).
**Comments**: `// to the end of the line` and `/* block */`.
**Strings** only show up inside `escreva`: there's no string type.
Token table: it goes straight into the report
Byteiro precedence table
In Byteiro, how is `a + b * 2 > 10 e ok` grouped?
Error: mixing arithmetic and logic is forbidden
Whatever is LOWER in the table binds tighter: first `*`, then `+`, then `>`, and last `e`. It's exactly the order the parser will follow in chapter 5.

Why `<-` for assignment? That way `=` is free to COMPARE and nobody writes `se (x = 1)` thinking it assigns. But there's a catch: `a<-1` is now `a <- 1` (assignment), not `a < -1`. It's the **longest lexeme** rule: the scanner always takes the longest possible token. Document that in the report!
The app's Lexi knows C: in C, `x<-1` is `x < -1`. In Byteiro the SAME text becomes `x <- 1`. The language specification is what defines the tokens.
Informal grammar (EBNF): { } = repeats 0+ times, [ ] = optional. Expressions are left for chapter 4.
Requiring braces in `se` shuts the door on the dangling else: there's never any doubt about which `se` a `senao` belongs to. Go and Rust make the same choice.
(1) **Lexical**: `#` doesn't belong to any token. (2) **Syntactic**: an expression should come after the `+`. (3) **Semantic**: the shape is right, but adding a `logico` makes no sense.
Lexical: malformed number '2x'
Syntactic: expected identifier, found '2'
It depends on how YOU specified the scanner, and you need to document it
None: 2x is a valid identifier

A scanner can cut `2x` into NUM(2) + ID(x) and let the syntactic phase complain, or refuse on the spot. Both are defensible! In Byteiro we decided it's a **lexical** error ('malformed number'). What costs points is not having decided.

Write the specification in the report BEFORE the code: token table, precedence, grammar, decisions (does case matter? can you redeclare in an inner block?). It becomes your map, and many professors grade that part.
Homework before chapter 3
Write 5 CORRECT Byteiro programs, each one exercising a feature (declaration, se/senao, enquanto, escreva, expressions).
Write 5 WRONG programs, with ONE error each: lexical, syntactic, undeclared, wrong type, redeclaration.
Next to each one, write down the expected output. Congratulations: you just started the test suite.
Token table ready? Then hand me the katana. Next chapter I slice everything.
From regex to DFA: the scanner
Each token is a regex, each regex is a DFA, and they all become ONE automaton, written in Java with a switch.
My trick: each token category is a **regular expression**; each regex becomes a **DFA**; and all the DFAs get glued into one big automaton, with a single start state.
Byteiro's regexes
ID (l = letter, d = digit; the _ was left out to fit the widget). Try 'l', 'ldl' and 'dl'.
NUM: at least one digit. Try 'd', 'ddd' and the empty string.
The '<' family (m = '<', h = '-', i = '=', g = '>'): accepts m, mh, mi, mg. Notice that the state after 'm' is already final: it's MENOR (less-than) alone.
OK, they're several DFAs. But how do I join them into one?

Create a state 0 with an arrow to the start of each DFA. Since the first characters are different (letter, digit, '<', '/'…), there are never two arrows with the same label leaving 0. It's still deterministic!
Byteiro's big automaton (draw the pretty version in the report!)
Piece of the transition table (* = returns the token without consuming the character)

Q: Does each reserved word need its own DFA? A: That would make a huge automaton. The classic trick: recognize everything as ID (state 1) and, at the end, check a table (HashMap) of reserved words. If it's there, it's a keyword; if not, it's an ID.
TipoToken.java and Token.java
Lexico.java (1/3): fields and helpers. '\0' plays the role of 'end of file'.
Lexico.java (2/3): the whole DFA: one case per state, just like the drawing
Lexico.java (3/3)
Input `x<y`. The DFA is in state 3 (already read '<') and sees the 'y'. What does the code do?
Consumes the 'y' and returns MENOR
Returns MENOR WITHOUT consuming the 'y'; it will be the start of the next token
Lexical error: '<y' isn't a token
Goes back to state 0 and drops the '<'

The 'y' is the drawing's 'outro*' (other): it only served to signal that the token was over. If you do `pos++` there, the 'y' vanishes and the parser gets `x <` followed by whatever comes next. It's the #1 bug in hand-written scanners.

Line counting: increment `linha` EVERYWHERE that consumes '\n', including inside the block comment (state 7). And don't count '\r': a file saved on Windows has '\r\n' at the end of each line; counting both doubles the line number in the messages.

`Character.isLetter` accepts 'ç', 'é', 'π'… If the specification says identifiers are ASCII only, swap it for `(c >= 'a' && c <= 'z') || (c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z')`. A small detail, but grading tests love it.
Byteiro's lexical errors (always with the line!)
Invalid character: `x <- 3 # 2;` → linha N: erro léxico: caractere inválido '#'
Malformed number: `12abc` → número malformado '12a'
Empty or unclosed character: `''` or `'A`
String that crosses the line: `"olá` + Enter
Comment `/*` without `*/` up to the end of the file

Many assignments ask for keywords that ignore case (`SE`, `Se`, `se`). It's ONE line: `RESERVADAS.getOrDefault(s.toLowerCase(), TipoToken.ID)`. Also decide whether identifiers ignore case (`Soma` = `soma`?), and document it.
TesteLexico.java: run it BEFORE writing a single line of the parser
Expected output: the comment vanished, `<-` and `<>` are ONE token each, and the line changes in the right place
Why does `proximo()` return one token at a time instead of a list with all of them?

Because a one-pass parser asks for tokens on demand, and a lexical error shows up exactly when the parser gets there. Building the whole list first also works (and lets you peek several tokens ahead); just make sure the lexical error still comes out with the right line.
Sliced! Now someone needs to check whether the pieces are in the right ORDER. Call Prof. Grammar.
Byteiro's LL(1) grammar
Remove left recursion, factor, and prove with FIRST/FOLLOW that one token is enough to decide.

Chapter 2's informal grammar is great for humans. To become recursive descent, it needs to be **LL(1)**: looking at ONE token, the parser knows which rule to use, with no backtracking and no guessing.
The three checks before programming
1. **No left recursion**: no `A -> A …`. (In Java that's infinite recursion.)
2. **Factored**: two alternatives of the same nonterminal can't start the same way.
3. **FIRST/FOLLOW with no overlap**: the FIRST sets of the alternatives are disjoint; and if an alternative can vanish (ε), the FIRST sets of the others don't overlap with FOLLOW.
First try: neat precedence… and left recursion in four places
What happens if you translate `Add -> Add + Mul` straight to Java (`void add() { add(); casaToken(MAIS); mul(); }`)?
It works normally
StackOverflowError: add() calls add() without consuming any token
It works, but with the wrong associativity
The first thing `add()` does is call `add()`: with the SAME token ahead. Nothing changes, so it calls itself forever until the stack blows up.
Before and after: A -> A α | β becomes A -> β A' and A' -> α A' | ε.

In EBNF it's even cleaner: `A -> A α | β` is the same as `A -> β { α }`: a β followed by zero or more α. And `{ }` becomes a **while** in Java. Bonus: the while builds the tree to the left, so `10 - 3 - 2` still gives 5.
Byteiro expressions in LL(1) EBNF, seven levels, seven Java methods
Cascade: the DEEPER the method, the STRONGER the operator. `ou` (or) lives at the top (groups last); `*` lives at the bottom (groups first).

And `Rel -> Add oprel Add | Add`? Both alternatives start with `Add`: a common prefix! Factoring: `Rel -> Add Rel'` and `Rel' -> oprel Add | ε`. In EBNF that's the optional `[ oprel exprAdd ]`, which becomes an **if** in Java.
If Byteiro had a procedure call `p(x);`, assignment and call would both start with `id`. And so would `se` with and without `senao`. See the factoring.
Byteiro statements in BNF (expressions summed up as E), ready for the LL(1) test
Compute FIRST and FOLLOW step by step. Notice: `senao` does NOT appear in FOLLOW(Senao).
No cell with two productions: it's LL(1)! The required block in `se` solved the dangling else.
In `Senao -> senao Bloco | ε`, when does the parser pick the ε alternative?
Never: ε is just decoration
When the current token is in FOLLOW(Senao); in practice, 'when it isn't senao'
When the current token is senao
When the file ends

The table puts ε in the FOLLOW(Senao) columns. In recursive descent code that becomes `if (eh(SENAO)) { … }` with no else: if it isn't `senao`, it consumes nothing, and if the token is junk, the next `casaToken` complains.

If your language allows `se (c) comando senao comando` WITHOUT braces, the cell [Senao, senao] gets two productions: that's the dangling else, and the grammar isn't LL(1). Practical fix in the parser: always match the `senao` with the nearest `se` (the greedy `if`), and document that decision.
Compute FIRST(comando) for the full Byteiro.
{ ID, se, enquanto, escreva, leia, `{`, inteiro, logico, caractere }: declarations start with the type, and a loose block starts with `{`. That set becomes the `comecaComando()` method in chapter 5.
FOLLOW of `{ comando }` inside the block: when does the repetition stop?
When the token isn't in FIRST(comando). In the right grammar, it can only be `}`: anything else makes `casaToken(FECHA_CHAVE)` complain with a precise message.

Q: Do I have to hand in the whole LL(1) table? A: It depends on the assignment. For recursive descent, what matters is the PROOF that there's no conflict: at each decision point in the code, the sets of tokens tested are disjoint. FIRST/FOLLOW in the report is exactly that proof.
The trio that shows up on the exam and in the project: left recursion → **while**; optional `[ ]` → **if**; repetition `{ }` → **while**. Memorize it and you'll translate any EBNF to Java in minutes.
Grammar… LL(1)… ready. Now… give me methods… to stack.
The recursive descent parser
One method per nonterminal, casaToken for terminals, if/while on the current token, and errors with a line number.
I am… Java's call stack. Each method you call… I push. When it returns… I pop. The parse tree… is the path I take.
The recipe (memorize it!)
One Java method for each nonterminal: `bloco()`, `comando()`, `expr()`…
Terminal on the right side → `casaToken(TIPO)`: checks and moves on.
Nonterminal on the right side → call its method.
Several alternatives → `if`/`switch` looking at the current token (the FIRST sets you computed).
The code the engine generates for the two-level cascade, and the call stack for `id + num * id`.
Sintatico.java (1/4), the infrastructure. Only `avanca()` touches `tok`!
Sintatico.java (2/4), programa, bloco and the comando() 'dispatcher'
Sintatico.java (3/4), the statements: read each method next to its EBNF rule
Sintatico.java (4/4), the precedence cascade: each level calls the one below
Why does `exprRel` use `if` and `exprAdd` use `while`?

Because `a + b + c` is allowed (repetition → while), but `a < b < c` isn't (relational operators are NON-associative → at most one → if). With the if, the extra `<` is left over and the parser complains about it.
`atribuicao()` matches ID(x) and `<-`, then calls `expr()`.
`expr` → `exprE` → `exprRel` → `exprAdd` → `exprMul` → `exprUn` → `primario()` matches `a`. Everything returns up to `exprAdd`.
`exprAdd` sees `+`: it moves on and calls `exprMul()`.
`exprMul` → `exprUn` → `primario` matches `2`. Back in `exprMul`, it sees `*`: moves on, `exprUn` → `primario` matches `b`.
`exprMul` sees no more `*`: returns. `exprAdd` sees no more `+`: returns. It goes back up to `atribuicao()`.
`atribuicao()` matches `;`. Notice: `2 * b` finished BEFORE the `+`: precedence came for free from the order of the calls.
Which message does our parser print for this program?
None: the program compiles

The parser only NOTICES the missing ';' when it sees the next token, the `x` on line 3. The message uses the line of the token found. If the assignment asks for 'the line of the error', that's what's expected; if it wants the line before, keep the line of the last token consumed.
Forgot `casaToken(TipoToken.EOF)` at the end of `programa()`? Then `programa t { } lixo lixo lixo` compiles 'successfully'. That's one of the first tests the grader runs.
Calling `lexico.proximo()` directly in several places 'loses' tokens: you move ahead twice without noticing. Golden rule: ONLY `avanca()` (and `casaToken`, which uses it) touches `tok`.
Now with Byteiro's statements: see the if/else of `Cmd` testing the FIRST sets of each alternative.

Q: What if the assignment asks to keep going after the first error? A: Panic mode: on an error, record the message and drop tokens until a safe point (`;` or `}`), then continue. For most projects, stopping at the first error is what's asked; check it.
Assignment with no expression: the parser complains, skips to a sync token and goes on to the escreva.

The parsers of GCC (C/C++), Clang, javac and Go are hand-written recursive descent, exactly the technique of your project. It gives full control over the error messages, and that's why professional compilers went back to it.

Classic question: 'write the recursive descent procedure for nonterminal X'. Follow the recipe: one if per alternative (with the FIRST sets), casaToken on terminals, a call on nonterminals, and an else with an error.
Symbol table and scopes
A stack of HashMaps: open a block = push, declare = put on top, use = search from the top down.
My parser accepts `x <- 1;` even without any `inteiro x;`. It doesn't remember ANYTHING!
It needs memory: the **symbol table**. And since Byteiro has blocks inside blocks, that memory needs **scopes**.
escopos.byt: read it top to bottom and follow each x
Tap each use and see which declaration it links to.
Nothing: y was declared in the program
Syntax error
When the inner block closed, its scope (with the y) was POPPED. The lookup on line 11 only finds the outer scope, where there's no y.
The stack of HashMaps in four operations
`inteiro x;` → **declare**: put x in the HashMap on TOP (if it's already there: redeclaration error).
use of `x` → **lookup**: search from the top down; the first one found wins (that's what makes the inner x hide the outer one).
TipoDado.java and Simbolo.java
TabelaSimbolos.java, the whole class fits on one screen
Lookup? I start… at the top. Not found? I go down a floor. Not found? Down again. Reached the ground… and nothing? Not declared.

Java trap: if you use `java.util.Stack` instead of `ArrayDeque`, for-each walks the stack from the BOTTOM UP! The lookup finds the OUTER x first and shadowing breaks without any error message. With `ArrayDeque` + `push`, iteration starts at the top.

Q: Why the label `x_1` and not just `x`? A: Two reasons. (1) The two x's in the example need TWO different addresses in `.data`: if both were `x`, MARS would complain about a duplicate label. (2) Variables named `b`, `j` or `add` clash with MIPS instructions and can confuse the assembler. The suffix fixes both.
In Sintatico: the parser now opens/closes scopes and records/looks up names

Where to call `usa(...)`? Everywhere an ID shows up without being a declaration: in `atribuicao()` (the target), in `leia()` and in `primario()`. In chapter 7 the returned `Simbolo` will tell the TYPE; in chapter 8, the memory LABEL.
The table during escopos.byt
Line 4, `{`: stack = [ {}, {x→x_0} ] (top on the left)
Line 6: lookup(x) finds x_1 on top, the caractere.
Line 10: lookup(x) finds x_0. Line 11: lookup(y) → null → semantic error!

Q: Can you declare an x in the inner block if an x already exists outside? A: It depends on the language! C allows it (shadowing). Java FORBIDS redeclaring a local variable in an inner block. Byteiro allows it. Either choice is fine, as long as it's written in the report and the compiler does what's written.
Classic question: given a program with nested blocks, say which declaration each use refers to (and which uses are errors). The Scope Hide-and-Seek game trains exactly that.

Real compilers keep much more in the Simbolo: size, offset in the activation record (relative to the frame pointer), whether it's a parameter, whether it was used (that's where the 'unused variable' warning comes from).
What if Byteiro got functions with local variables?

Each function would open a scope for parameters and locals, and the locals would live on the runtime STACK (frame offset), not in `.data`, so each recursive call has its own copy. See the activation records area in the Code Forge.
Type checking
Each expression method returns the TYPE of what it recognized; assignment and condition check the rules.
Look at this: `logico ok; ok <- 3 * 'A';` gets through my parser! Shouldn't it be an error?

It should. The shape is right; the MEANING isn't. The idea: each expression method stops being `void` and starts **returning the type** of the piece it recognized. The type goes up from the leaf to the root; it's a **synthesized attribute**.
The type going up the tree (the widget uses C syntax: `&&` is our `e`; a and b are integers, ok is logico).
Type rules for Byteiro expressions (they go in the report)
Assignment rules: implicit conversion only in the direction that loses no information
With `inteiro n; caractere c;`, which of these lines gives a semantic error?

`c + 1` is numeric + numeric → **inteiro**. Storing an inteiro in a caractere is forbidden (it might not fit). But `n <- c + 1` and `n <- c` are fine: caractere goes up to inteiro without losing anything.
Type helpers in Sintatico
The cascade now returns TipoDado, the same skeleton as chapter 5
Tree leaves: literals have a fixed type; identifiers ask the symbol table
Statements: assignment checks compatibility; se/enquanto require a logico condition

Top bug: in `exprRel`, forgetting `t = TipoDado.LOGICO`. Then `a < b` 'has type' inteiro, `se (a < b)` gives a condition error and `x <- a < b` gets through as an inteiro. A comparison ALWAYS produces logico, whatever the type of its sides.
`exprAdd`: numeric + numeric → INTEIRO.
`primario` of n → INTEIRO. `exprRel`: INTEIRO > INTEIRO → LOGICO.
`exprE`: LOGICO and LOGICO → LOGICO.
`atribuicao`: podeAtribuir(LOGICO, LOGICO) → ✓.
It compiles: n different from 0 is true, as in C
Semantic error: the condition must be logico
Syntax error: expected a comparison
It compiles with a warning
Byteiro is 'Java style': a condition has to be logico. Syntactically `(n)` is a perfectly good expression; what stops it is the type check in `condicao()`. Write `se (n <> 0)`.

Each language chooses. C converts integers to booleans without asking; JavaScript makes `'5' * 2` give 10; Java requires a boolean in the if. None of them is 'right'; what matters is that the rule is written down and the compiler obeys it.

Q: Does the caractere → inteiro conversion generate any instruction? A: No! The character already lives in memory as a number (65). The 'conversion' exists only in the type table. In C, though, int → float generates a real MIPS instruction (`cvt.s.w`), because the representation changes.
Five semantic tests with the expected output; copy them into testes/erro/

A **synthesized** attribute goes up (the expression's type, computed from the children). An **inherited** attribute goes down: in `inteiro a, b, c;` the type is passed as a parameter to `declaraUm(t)` for each ID. Your project has both: mention it in the report!
Does type checking need to be a separate phase, with a tree?

Not necessarily. In the one-pass scheme it lives INSIDE the parser (syntax-directed translation). Building an AST and then visiting it is also valid, and makes bigger optimizations easier, but it takes more code. For the project, one pass is the shortest path.
Generating MIPS for MARS
Expressions in temporary registers, variables in .data, labels for se/enquanto, syscalls for printing.
Forge time. Each method, besides checking types, now **emits** its piece of assembly. First, the minimal MIPS kit the generator uses.
The project's MIPS cheat sheet: this alone compiles all of Byteiro
The generator's infrastructure (inside Sintatico, Java 17)
Leaves and unary operators: each leaf takes ONE new register
Binary operations: the result stays in the LEFT register
How many $t registers are busy AT THE SAME TIME, at the peak, when generating `a + b * c`?
Assignment, se and enquanto: the translation scheme with labels
The two templates you'll draw in the report
Input and output with syscall

`div` with three operands, `rem`, `seq`, `sne`, `sgt`, `sle` and `sge` are **pseudo-instructions**: MARS expands them into real instructions. They work perfectly on MARS, but if the assignment forbids pseudo-instructions, swap them for `div`+`mflo`/`mfhi` and for combinations of `slt` with `xori`.
contagem.byt from chapter 2 again…
…and the COMPLETE saida.asm our compiler generates for it
Running it on MARS
Download MARS (a .jar, e.g. `Mars4_5.jar`); it needs Java installed.
GUI: `java -jar Mars4_5.jar` → File › Open → `saida.asm`.
Run › Assemble (F3). An error here = YOUR generator emitted something that isn't valid MIPS.
Run › Go (F5). The output shows up in the **Run I/O** tab: `soma = 30`.
Command line (great for automatic tests): `java -jar Mars4_5.jar nc saida.asm` (nc = no copyright notice).
If `novoRotulo` always returned `"fimse"`, without the counter, what would happen in a program with two `se`?
Nothing: labels can repeat
MARS refuses at assembly: label defined twice
The second se would jump to the first fimse
Java gives a compile error

A label is a NAME for an address: two equal ones are ambiguous, and the assembler refuses. That's why there's a global counter, and why every project test should have `se` inside `se` and `enquanto` inside `enquanto`.

Q: Why `.word` (4 bytes) even for logico and caractere? A: Simplicity: everything uses `lw`/`sw`, with no alignment to think about. You can use `.byte` with `lb`/`sb` for caractere; it saves 3 bytes per variable and adds a pile of special cases. In a project, uniformity wins.
This style (every variable in memory: load, operate, store) is similar to what GCC does with `-O0`. Real compilers only get clever (variables living in registers) when you turn on optimization.
Simple optimizations and a test suite
Fold constants, cut dead code, a light peephole, and tests that prove nothing broke.
It does: unless the compiler computes it first. That's **constant folding**: if both sides of an operation are known at compile time, do the math in Java and emit only the result.
Look at the instruction for `2 * 3`: both operands are constants. The compiler can do that math by itself.

The trick to fit this into a one-pass generator: `Res` gets a third field, `constante`. A numeric leaf **reserves** the register, but **postpones** the `li`. If the next operation also receives a constant, the math is done in Java and no code comes out. Only when someone really needs the value in a register is the `li` emitted.
Constant folding: Res can now carry a known value

In the rest of the generator there are three mechanical swaps: (1) in `primario`, literals become `return constante(tipo, valor);` instead of `novoTemp()` + `li`; (2) each `binaria(instr, esq, dir); esq = new Res(...)` becomes `esq = binaria(op, instr, esq, dir, tipo);`; (3) every place that used `x.reg()` to emit (`sw`, `move`, `beq`, `xori`, `sub`) now uses `noRegistrador(x)`. In unary operators: if the operand is constant, return `-c` or `1 - c` without emitting anything.
Six instructions become two
Yes, 2 + 3 gets folded
No: the tree is (a + 2) + 3 and no operation has TWO constant sides
No, because `a` is a variable and spoils the whole expression
Yes, but only if `a` is zero

`+` associates to the left: first `a + 2` (one side variable), then `(…) + 3`. But `2 + 3 + a` becomes `5 + a`. Real compilers reorder (reassociation) to catch the first case, a good piece of 'future work' for the report.

Never fold `x / 0` with a Java computation: it throws ArithmeticException and YOUR COMPILER crashes with a stack trace. Return `null` (don't fold) and leave the error for runtime, or emit a warning with the line. And notice: Java and MIPS truncate integer division the same way (`-7 / 2 = -3`), so folding doesn't change the result.
Dead code elimination: the block is still ANALYZED (errors still show up), it just doesn't generate MIPS

Q: Why not just skip the tokens of the dead block? A: Because the block still has to be RIGHT: a syntax or type error inside `se (falso) { … }` is still an error. That's why it goes through the parser normally, just with the 'pen' turned off. (The string of a dead `escreva` still goes to .data, harmlessly.)
Peephole optimization: a 2-instruction window sliding over the finished .asm
Optimized? Then… prove… nothing… broke.
A test suite that catches real bugs
**Precedence and associativity**: `escreva(2 + 3 * 4);` → 14; `escreva((2 + 3) * 4);` → 20; `escreva(10 - 3 - 2);` → 5 (not 9!).
**Loops**: an `enquanto` that runs 0 times, 1 time and N times.
**Nesting**: `se` inside `se` inside `enquanto` (unique labels!).
**Scopes**: shadowing (inner and outer x with different values; print both).
**Errors**: one file per error message: lexical, syntactic, each semantic rule.
**Edge cases**: empty file, comment only, unclosed comment, string with a space, `'A' + 1` printed as a number.
Practice checking by hand: with a=4, b=2, c=3, d=5, the result must be -12. Compute it BEFORE running.
Automatic regression tests (Linux/macOS/Git Bash). Generate each .esperado (expected output) ONCE, check it by hand, and freeze it.
That's **regression** testing: after each optimization or fix, run the whole suite. That's exactly how GCC and LLVM work, with thousands of test programs running on every change.
Exams love: 'apply constant folding and dead code elimination to this three-address code'. Fold first, then see which branches ended up with a constant condition, then cut what's never reached.
Why is generating the `.esperado` by running your own compiler dangerous?

Because if the compiler is wrong, you freeze the error as the 'right answer'. Check each `.esperado` by hand (or compute it before running) the first time; after that it protects you against regressions.

**Wrong line in the messages.** The most common mistake of all. Causes: not counting '\n' inside a block comment, also counting '\r', or using the line of the PREVIOUS token when the assignment wants the one of the token found (or vice versa). Have an error test AFTER a multi-line comment.

**Leaking registers.** Forgetting a `liberaTemp()` doesn't break small programs… until the 11th statement, when 'out of registers' shows up out of nowhere. Test with a program of 30 assignments in a row.
One 'assert' line that saves a night of debugging
Someone wrote in the scanner: `if (lexema == "senao") …`. What happens?
It always works
Sometimes it doesn't recognize the word: `==` on Strings compares REFERENCES, not content
It only works on Windows

In Java, `==` between Strings asks 'is it the same object?'. The lexeme built in a StringBuilder is a NEW object, so the comparison fails. Use `equals`: or, even better, the HashMap of reserved words and enums as in chapter 3.

**Colliding labels and names.** Two nested `se` generating the same label, or a variable called `main`, `j` or `b` turning into a raw label. The counter in the labels and the `_N` suffix on variables fix it; have a test with `inteiro j, b, main;`.

Academic integrity: copying a classmate's compiler, one from a previous semester, or asking an AI to write it without understanding it shows up at the oral exam in two minutes, and usually zeroes the project. Use this guide as a MAP: the examples are Byteiro, your language is different, and the code has to be yours.
Practice the oral exam out loud, one member questioning the other. The questions below are the classic ones.
Oral exam: 'Why is your grammar LL(1)?'

Because it has no left recursion, it's factored and, in each nonterminal with alternatives, the FIRST sets are disjoint (and don't overlap with FOLLOW when there's ε). Show the FIRST/FOLLOW table from the report and point to the matching `if`/`switch` in the code.
Oral exam: 'Show where the type of `a + 'b'` is computed.'
In `exprAdd`: `primario` returns INTEIRO for `a` and CARACTERE for `'b'`; both are numeric, so the result is INTEIRO. No extra instruction: the character is already a number in memory.
Oral exam: 'How does your scanner know `<-` is a single token?'
State 3 of the DFA: after reading '<', it looks at the next character. If it's '-', it consumes it and returns ATRIB (longest lexeme). If it's anything else, it returns MENOR without consuming.
Oral exam: 'What happens to the scope stack when the enquanto block closes?'
`fechaEscopo()` pops the block's HashMap: the names declared there stop being visible. But the `.word` stays in `.data`: scope is a COMPILE-time rule, not a memory rule.
